title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
oneLinerQuestion: Find the lowest common ancestor of two target nodes in a general binary tree.
explanation:
Problem Intuition: The Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) of a Binary Tree problem asks us to identify the deepest shared ancestor node that has both target nodes p and q as descendants (where a node can be a descendant of itself). Without the ordering guarantees of a Binary Search Tree, we cannot decide paths based on node values alone. Instead, we use a bottom-up post-order DFS traversal. When a subtree returns a non-null node, it signals that either p, q, or their already-resolved LCA was found within that branch. If a node receives non-null answers from both its left and right subtrees, it acts as the meeting junction and is the LCA. If only one branch returns a non-null node, that result simply propagates upward toward the root.

- Step 1: Base Case & Target Match Guard — If `root === null`, the branch has terminated without finding either target, so return `null`. If `root === p` or `root === q`, return `root` immediately. Returning `root` directly propagates the target node upwards without needing to search its descendants, because even if the other target lies below it, this node is by definition the LCA.

- Step 2: Post-Order Recursive Descent — We recurse down both child branches: `const left = lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q)` and `const right = lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q)`.

- Step 3: Divergent Subtree Convergence Check — We inspect the results returned from both subtrees: `if (left !== null && right !== null) return root`. If both sides return non-null values, p and q reside in separate subtrees beneath `root`, establishing `root` as the lowest common ancestor.

- Step 4: Unilateral Result Propagation — If only one subtree returned a non-null node, it means either both targets lie within that single branch or only one target has been found so far. We forward that non-null reference up the call stack: `if (left !== null) return left; if (right !== null) return right;`.

- Step 5: Absence Fallback — If both `left === null` and `right === null`, neither p nor q exists within the current subtree, so return `null`.

- Step 6: Final Result Return — The upward propagation converges at the root of the tree, returning the reference to the lowest common ancestor node.

- Complexity & Memory Guarantees — Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the total number of nodes in the binary tree, as every node is visited at most once during traversal. Space Complexity: O(H) auxiliary space on the call stack, where H is the height of the tree (O(log N) for balanced trees, O(N) for degenerate trees).
pseudoCode:
FUNCTION lowestCommonAncestor(root, p, q):
    IF root IS NULL OR root == p OR root == q THEN RETURN root
    left = lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q)
    right = lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q)
    IF left IS NOT NULL AND right IS NOT NULL THEN RETURN root
    RETURN IF left IS NOT NULL THEN left ELSE right
END FUNCTION

Line 3: Recurse left from root 3 to Node(5). Node 5 matches target p! Return Node(5) upward.
Line 4: Recurse right from root 3 to Node(1). Node 1 matches target q! Return Node(1) upward.
Line 5: At root Node(3): left return is 5 (not NULL) and right return is 1 (not NULL). Both branches returned target nodes!
Line 6: Fork confirmed at root. Node 3 is the Lowest Common Ancestor. RETURN Node(3).
